catalog_locator: p.3, section 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)'; p.4, 'Conventions: Orthographic'
catalog_quote: Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length) Stress is non phonemic - it generally falls on the last, or second and fourth syllables of a word, except that it preferentially goes to syllables with long vowels or diphthongs. Vowel length is important, as the above examples show. ... Tone steps may distinguish meaning in some homonyms, but tone does not appear to be important. ... [p.4] <w> and <y> are sometimes written where they may not be the actual phonemes. This is done to show stress and syllabification, which are not always predictable. Within words, they are written consistently at the beginning of a stressed syllable, or in vowel sequences to show syllable breaks.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: both deciding passages are verbatim in the held OPD PDF at p.3 ('Suprasegmentals') and p.4 ('Conventions: Orthographic'), exactly as cited. (2) Deciding source: a 5-page SIL Organised Phonology Data sheet (2004 print of Oates 1994 data). Thin in absolute terms, but it is the best description of Ninggerum stress that exists: Glottolog's MED is 'wordlist or less', OLAC and web searches surface no grammar, phonology paper, dissertation or instrumental study for nxr, and the two older primary remarks are wordlist-based — Healey 1964 p.61 (held; hedges toward possible phonemic accent, no rule) and Voorhoeve 1975 p.384 (fetched sources now: 'a primary stress seems to occur always on the last syllable').
